newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Solana's central Asian trip points up role of PFP.
newsitem.headline: Solana's central Asian trip points up role of PFP.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana's visit to central Asia has highlighted the growing importance of the alliance's Partnership for Peace (PFP) programme -- increasingly seen as a key ingredient of a new European security order.
NATO, which plans only a limited expansion eastwards, is keen for a revamped and reinvigorated PFP to become a permanent feature of Europe's post-Cold War security architecture.
"We want to show these countries that PFP is not just a central European club or a waiting-room for NATO but is set to become a significant structure in its own right," one alliance source said.
Some 27 countries across Europe have now signed up to PFP, created in 1994 to fill a vaccum following the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Many countries, particularly front-runners like Poland and Hungary, have always seen it as a way of preparing themselves for eventual NATO membership.
Others, including Russia and Ukraine, more as a way of boosting cooperation with former enemies.

"PFP has enabled us to create a European military union, to allow ad hoc military alliances to be created... without PFP the Stabilisation Force (SFOR) in Bosnia would have been far harder to get off the ground," said one diplomat, referring to the multinational peacekeeping force in Bosnia.

Major Western powers hope a beefed-up PFP, which allows for joint exercises and exchanges of officers and information with NATO countries, will sugar the pill for countries like the Baltic states set to be left out of alliance enlargement.

Only a few weeks before his current trip to Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan, Solana visited the Caucasus, drawing fire from Moscow which sees former Soviet Republics as its own zone of influence.

NATO argues however Solana's foreign forays to countries which have no hope, and often no interest, in joining the alliance are designed to underline the importance of the partnership programme in its own right.
Shortly after taking office, Solana pledged to visit all the partnership countries -- a promise he has now almost fulfilled.

Alliance sources said Solana would discuss ways of sponsoring more PFP activities in central Asia and ways of streamlining current activities to bring everything from political dialogue to disaster relief under one roof.

NATO hopes to create an Atlantic Partnership Council to cover the political aspects of PFP at the same time as inviting a handful of former communist countries, led by Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, to join the alliance in July.

They hope a special summit in Madrid will also endorse a new NATO-Russia document setting out a new relationship between the old foes and launch a PFP-2 with a more adventurous programme and enhanced financial status.

Moscow appears ready to accept NATO's enlargement, albeit reluctantly, but remains implacably opposed to republics of the former Soviet Union, such as the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, joining the Western Alliance.
"That once again points to PFP having more and more of a role," one independent analyst said.
